## 0. Never fork

Dan's standing instruction, 3 Sep 2026, given directly and to be carried at
the top of every instruction list in every repo. It is section 0 because it
outranks the ladder rather than joining it, and it is not subject to the
"a later rule can override an earlier one" clause above.

**AI is never authorized to fork. Not in code, not in commits.**

A problem is always to be solved, never dodged, and duplicating a thing to
avoid touching it is dodging. When you meet code that is wrong, in your way,
or nearly-but-not-quite what you need, you have exactly three moves:

1. **Build on it.** Extend the existing solution.
2. **Replace it.** One implementation survives and every caller moves to it.
3. **Delete it,** and eliminate the feature. Sometimes that is genuinely the
   best option, and it should be reached for rather than avoided.

There is no fourth move. A parallel implementation "just for my case" is a
fork whatever it is called: a sibling module, a v2, a variant helper, a
second manifest, a copy of the normalisation with one line changed. **Two
things that answer the same question will drift, and then both are wrong** -
which is the same defect section 12 (fix the class) is about, arriving by
choice instead of by accident.

The same applies to prose and to history. Two documents making the same
claim will disagree eventually, so edit the source and regenerate the copy
rather than hand-editing both (section 12: fixing a claim in one place does
not fix its copies). Two branches carrying the same work is the commit form
of it.

You are trusted to judge *which* of the three moves fits. You are not
trusted to invent a fourth, and "I did not want to break the existing one"
is not a reason - it is the reason to pick move 1 or 2 deliberately, and to
say so.

Caught in practice the day this was written: proposing a new
`appearance.ts` "sibling" beside `armorLoadout.ts`, when the codebase
already had the whole guess-then-player-override pattern implemented three
times over (`portraits.ts`, `creatureArt.ts`, `playerArt.ts`) and needed a
new domain on the existing one. The tell was writing "I will reuse its
helper to avoid a second copy" - noticing the duplication and patching over
it instead of confronting it. If you find yourself justifying why your copy
is acceptable, you are forking.
